chunks.text: [Page 1] Hop-Hop Relation-aware Graph Neural Networks Li Zhang 1 Yan Ge1 Haiping Lu 1 Abstract Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) are widely used in graph representation learning. However, most GNN methods are designed for either homoge- neous or heterogeneous graphs. In this paper, we propose a new model, Hop-Hop Relation-aware Graph Neural Network (HHR-GNN), to unify rep- resentation learning for these two types of graphs. HHR-GNN learns a personalized receptive ﬁeld for each node by leveraging knowledge graph embedding to learn relation scores between the central node’s representations at different hops. In neighborhood aggregation, our model simul- taneously allows for hop-aware projection and aggregation. This mechanism enables the central node to learn a hop-wise neighborhood mixing that can be applied to both homogeneous and het- erogeneous graphs. Experimental results on ﬁve benchmarks show the competitive performance of our model compared to state-of-the-art GNNs, e.g., up to 13K faster in terms of time cost per training epoch on large heterogeneous graphs. 1. Introduction Graphs, such as social networks, knowledge graphs and citation networks, are ubiquitous data structures capturing interactions between individual nodes. They can be broadly divided into homogeneous (one type of nodes and edges) and heterogeneous (multiple types of nodes and edges) graphs (Yang et al., 2020). Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have been widely used in graph representation learning and achieved impressive performance in various applications, such as academic citation networks (Kipf & Welling, 2017; Velickovic et al., 2018), social networks (Hamilton et al., 2017), knowledge graphs (Schlichtkrull et al., 2018) and recommender systems (van den Berg et al., 2017; Ying et al., 2018). A general GNN framework mainly consists of two key steps: neighborhood aggregation and feature transformation. In neighborhood aggregation, a given node ﬁrst aggregates (such as sum, mean and pooling) its neighbors, followed by a linear mapping or a multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs) in the feature transformation step to get the node’s new representation (Hornik et al., 1989). Most existing GNNs follow a neighborhood aggregation or “message passing” scheme. Graph convolutional network (GCN) is derived from spectral graph convolutions (Shu- man et al., 2013; Bruna et al., 2014; Cho et al., 2014) and simpliﬁes the K-localized Chebynet (Defferrard et al., 2016; Bronstein et al., 2017) by only aggregating one-hop neigh- bors. Graph Attention Networks (GAT) (Velickovic et al., 2018) learns to assign different edge weights at each layer. However, limiting node’s receptive ﬁelds to only one-hop neihgbors seems arbitrary (Klicpera et al., 2019). Some works generalize GCN to incorporate higher-order neigh- [Page 6] Hop-Hop Relation-aware Graph Neural Networks bors. GraphSAGE (Hamilton et al., 2017) aggregates neigh- bors sampled from a ﬁxed-length random work. MixHop and Lanczosnet [18] explore multi-scale information based on powers of adjacency matrix.
